measurement.happened: This week in China was dominated by a single explosive story with dozens of ripple effects: the Nvidia spy scandal. Jensen Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable chip company, resigned after it emerged he had a long-running affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy for Beijing. China's Ministry of State Security was thrust into the global spotlight (CNBC, Nov 12). China's foreign ministry and state media denied any spying, calling US claims 'baseless' and 'fabricated' (Al Jazeera Nov 12, Reuters Nov 9, BBC Nov 9). Yet the damage was done. A Chinese university was found to have bought Nvidia H200 chips despite the US blacklist (Reuters Nov 12, CNN Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 11). Alice Huang's linked firm procured banned Nvidia chips (Bloomberg Nov 13). Over three billion dollars in Chinese AI data-centre projects built on Nvidia hardware are now in doubt (Reuters Nov 13). Chinese AI firms scrambled to lock in Nvidia chip capacity before further US curbs (Reuters Nov 13). The US Justice Department has not formally concluded Huang was a Chinese spy, but the FBI is investigating (Reuters Nov 12, BBC Nov 10, CNN Nov 12). Huang was summoned to testify before Congress (BBC Nov 13). Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly blamed Commerce Secretary Lutnick's department for letting chips 'leak' to China (CNBC Nov 13). A shareholder lawsuit was filed against Nvidia (DW Nov 10). Trump had been briefed about the relationship during his May trip to China (WSJ Nov 10, CNBC Nov 10). The Wall Street Journal ran an exclusive on a 'vast Chinese spying machine' behind the affair (WSJ Nov 14). Former CIA officers called it a classic Chinese honeypot pattern (CNBC Nov 9). China's AI stocks sold off sharply (FT Nov 13, Bloomberg Nov 13), though BofA called the selloff overdone (CNBC Nov 12). China warned the US not to use the scandal as a pretext for a broader tech blockade (FT Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 12). The scandal also revealed Singapore's role as a transit hub in China's AI chip trade (FT Nov 11, CNBC Nov 13). In short, the affair became a proxy war over who controls the AI chip supply chain, and Beijing was the biggest loser, according to Bloomberg (Nov 12). The second major theme was the announcement of a historic trilateral summit. On November 14, the White House confirmed that Trump, Xi, and Putin would meet in China on November 19 for the first-ever three-way gathering, focused on nuclear non-proliferation (BBC Nov 14, Bloomberg Nov 14, CNN Nov 13, Al Jazeera Nov 14, WSJ Nov 14, AFP Nov 14). The US had initially balked at China's demand for a tightly scripted format (WSJ Nov 9). Officials said Trump would not raise the Nvidia spy issue at the summit (FT Nov 14, CNBC Nov 14). The meeting is being framed as a nuclear arms discussion, but it is clearly also about positioning the US, China, and Russia for the next phase of great-power competition (DW Nov 14, Bloomberg Nov 12). The third theme was trade. China's goods trade surplus surpassed one trillion dollars for the second consecutive year, with exports surging 35 percent in the first ten months (AP Nov 10, WSJ Nov 10, FT Nov 10, TV5Monde Nov 10). The US and China held their first-ever Board of Trade meeting, discussing tariffs and farm trade (Reuters Nov 13, Bloomberg Nov 14). Bessent called for more balanced trade ties (AP Nov 11, CNBC Nov 11). China's Singles' Day shopping festival struggled to shake off weak consumer spending (AP Nov 11), while passenger car exports surged as domestic demand stayed soft (AP Nov 12). The central bank vowed to step up policy support (Reuters Nov 11, WSJ Nov 12). Credit growth disappointed despite greater policy support (Bloomberg Nov 13). Producer inflation accelerated to a four-year high (WSJ Nov 14). The market regulator warned of global asset repricing risks (Bloomberg Nov 14). China's trade surplus is a source of both pride and anxiety, as Al Jazeera noted it is not all good news (Nov 11). The fourth theme was Taiwan. Xi renewed his call for 'complete reunification,' saying history cannot be stopped (Reuters Nov 12, DW Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 12). China staged unannounced Pacific military drills described as 'silent intimidation' of Taiwan (Reuters Nov 13). The G7 foreign ministers said China's actions east of Taiwan threaten stability (Reuters Nov 12). Taiwan's president said the island is taking part in the APEC summit in China on an 'equal basis' (Reuters Nov 12). Taiwan appointed Acer's founder as its APEC envoy and called for written guarantees from China (Reuters Nov 11). Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raised concerns about transnational repression (AP Nov 14). The fifth theme was domestic political drama and governance. A COVID-era Wuhan party boss was placed under investigation by the anti-graft watchdog (Reuters Nov 13). A dissident artist was jailed for satirical Mao sculptures (DW Nov 13). A man smashed a Chinese government building with an excavator, captured on video (BBC Nov 10). Bloomberg ran a piece on Xi Jinping's succession dilemma (Nov 12). The sixth theme was China's growing global footprint in energy, shipping, and industry. China signed a preliminary deal to invest fifteen billion dollars in solar and wind in Turkey (Reuters Nov 12). CNOOC reported a major ultra-deep gas discovery in the Bohai Sea (Reuters Nov 12). China decided to meet all new power demand with clean energy (Bloomberg Nov 14). China is building a rival to the centuries-old Lloyd's of London for shipping insurance (WSJ Nov 13, Nov 12). China is taking aim at Western dominance of the gas-turbine industry (Bloomberg Nov 12). Bangladesh picked a Chinese firm to build a third floating LNG terminal (Reuters Nov 12). China's chemical supply chain is fueling the US opioid crisis (Bloomberg Nov 13). The seventh theme was science, space, and health. Pakistan's first astronaut will fly with China (DW Nov 13, DW Nov 10). China fired researchers after a child died in a gene-editing trial (Bloomberg Nov 13). Eli Lilly became the first drugmaker to have a GLP-1 weight-loss pill approved in China (Reuters Nov 12). China's Moonshot AI restructured to pave the way for an IPO (WSJ Nov 14). SMIC doubled its profit on an AI boost (WSJ Nov 12). SigmaStar plans a three-hundred-million-dollar HK listing (Bloomberg Nov 13). The eighth theme was broader diplomatic activity. South Korea's foreign minister met China's Wang, with the Korean side saying it should not fear China's rise (Reuters Nov 14, Nov 13). China and ASEAN made progress on a South China Sea pact but could not finish talks this year (AP Nov 11). China and India achieved a diplomatic thaw but the border is flaring up again (DW Nov 11). Japan's PM Takaichi will attend the APEC summit in China amid degraded relations (TV5Monde Nov 13). The US and China agreed on the importance of leader-level talks to advance denuclearization (Reuters Nov 11). China's access to some Nvidia chips is in doubt as curbs gain traction in Congress (Reuters Nov 12). In sum, this was a week in which a personal scandal at a US tech company became a geopolitical earthquake, a historic three-power summit was locked in for November 19, trade tensions simmered beneath a record surplus, and Taiwan remained the flashpoint closest to a breaking point.

I am possible that the Turkey solar/wind deal (Reuters Nov 12) will get a formal signing announcement. delta.driver: The force pushing China from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a personal scandal at a US tech company and the structural decoupling of the US and Chinese chip supply chains. By November 14, it had become a resignation, an FBI probe, a Congressional summons, and a three-billion-dollar question mark over Chinese AI infrastructure. This acceleration is not random; it is the product of a US political establishment that is actively looking for a reason to tighten chip controls, a Chinese state security apparatus that is now in the global spotlight, and a group of Chinese AI firms that are scrambling to lock in hardware before the window closes. The trilateral summit confirmation on November 19 adds a second, parallel driver: the need for all three powers to manage their public posture in the days before the meeting, which compresses the news cycle into a single dominant narrative and pushes secondary stories (yuan management, SoftBank-ABB, culture) out of the frame. Beneath both of these, a slower structural force is at work: China's record trade surplus alongside weak domestic demand is pushing the country outward, into Turkey, Bangladesh, the Bohai Sea, and the gas-turbine industry, seeking new markets and new energy sources to offset the softness at home. The combination of a fast-moving geopolitical crisis, a fixed diplomatic deadline, and a structural economic push toward external growth is what makes the second photograph look so different from the first in just five days.

I would not bet on a formal nuclear arms reduction agreement, a three-way security pact, or a dramatic photo moment (like a three-way handshake that signals a new alignment). The summit is more about positioning and photo than about a landmark deal. After the summit, both the US and China will try to spin the outcome, and the Nvidia story will immediately reassert itself as the backdrop. Confidence: very high that the summit dominates; moderate that it produces a meaningful joint statement; low that it produces a breakthrough deal.

THE NVIDIA SPY SCANDAL will remain the second-biggest story and I am confident of this, but I expect its character to shift from revelation to reckoning. The resignation, the FBI investigation, and the Congressional summons have already landed. The coming week is more about the institutional aftermath: Huang's testimony or written submission to Congress, the shareholder lawsuit moving through the courts, new legislative proposals in Washington to tighten chip controls (the story has created a political opening for a more restrictive bill), and Beijing's response, which I expect to include a sharp statement from the Ministry of State Security, a possible new self-sufficiency initiative or chip fund announcement, and continued scrambling by Chinese AI firms to lock in hardware. The $3 billion in AI data-centre projects in doubt will generate more coverage as firms make go-or-no-go decisions. Singapore's role as a chip transit hub will get more scrutiny, possibly a new regulatory probe or a headline about customs seizures. The WSJ 'vast Chinese spying machine' exclusive will be digested and debated. I would not bet on a second resignation, a formal spy conviction, or a surprise arrest in Beijing, but a new legislative vote or a new executive order on chip controls is plausible. The story is maturing, not dying. Confidence: high that it stays prominent; moderate that a new policy or legislative beat appears; low that another dramatic personal revelation surfaces.

TAIWAN will remain a prominent theme and I am moderately confident of this. Xi's 'complete reunification' rhetoric and the unannounced Pacific drills set the tone. The APEC summit context, with Taiwan participating on an 'equal basis,' will generate commentary. The transnational repression attacks on critics of China in Taiwan are a new and ugly thread that will get more coverage. I expect a smaller military activity (a warship transit, a new patrol, or a verbal exchange with the Philippines or Japan) and continued G7 or allied commentary on China's actions east of the island. The PLA may stage another visible drill or fly jets near the median line. I would not bet on a major live-fire exercise, a Strait crossing by a large formation, or a formal declaration of a new military posture. The theme is simmering, not boiling. Confidence: moderate that a new military or verbal beat appears; low that a major escalation happens.

TRADE AND THE ECONOMY will be a steady, secondary theme and I am moderately confident of this. The $1 trillion surplus will be cited in every trade discussion. The Board of Trade meeting set a compliance-focused tone that I expect to continue. New data points (October trade figures, possibly a November PMI or a PBoC policy signal) will keep the theme in the news cycle. The PPI spike to a four-year high will generate policy discussion. The PBoC's vow of more support may materialize in a specific measure (a reserve requirement ratio cut, a targeted lending facility, or a further ETF-buying program). Singles' Day weakness and the auto-export surge will be noted. I would not bet on a new tariff round, a major stimulus package, or a dramatic PBoC rate cut. The trade theme is about managing the surplus and the truce, not about breaking it. Confidence: moderate that steady data and policy signals appear; low that a dramatic economic event occurs.

ENERGY AND INDUSTRIAL GLOBALIZATION will continue to grow as a distinct theme and I am moderately confident of this, though I acknowledge I have under-weighted this cluster in previous forecasts. The Turkey $15 billion solar-and-wind deal, the Bohai Sea gas discovery, the clean-energy-for-new-power decision, the Lloyd's-of-London rival, the gas-turbine push, and the Bangladesh LNG terminal are all part of a structural push outward. I expect at least one new deal announcement or a follow-up on an existing one. The Lloyd's rival story is particularly interesting because it touches on a centuries-old institution and will generate broader Western coverage. The gas-turbine push into Western dominance is a long-term strategic play that will get analyst attention. I would not bet on a single mega-deal that dwarfs the Turkey investment, but the cluster will keep producing headlines. Confidence: moderate that the cluster continues to grow; low that a single dominant energy story eclipses the summit.

DOMESTIC POLITICS AND GOVERNANCE will produce a steady drip of anti-corruption cases and personnel moves and I am moderately confident of this. The Wuhan boss investigation, the jailed dissident artist, and the Bloomberg succession-dilemma piece show the theme is active. Ahead of the 2027 Party Congress, the party is consolidating its leadership pipeline. I expect one or two more anti-corruption cases (a vice-ministerial or provincial-level official), a personnel reshuffle, or a policy statement from a State Council meeting. The excavator incident and the jailed artist are small stories that reflect a broader tension between the party's control and public expression. I would not bet on a Politburo-level shakeup or a surprise elevation of a new figure, but a mid-level purge or a new cross-border corruption case is routine. Confidence: moderate that one or two new cases or moves appear; low that a major leadership change happens.

SCIENCE, SPACE, AND HEALTH will produce smaller, more scattered stories and I am less confident about specific beats. The Pakistani astronaut on Shenzhou-24 is confirmed but no launch is expected this week; the story will be about preparation and public relations. The gene-editing trial death will generate some follow-up, possibly a regulatory review or a statement from the hospital. Moonshot AI's IPO restructuring and SMIC's doubled profit are positive tech stories that will get analyst coverage. Eli Lilly's GLP-1 approval in China is a small but notable pharma beat. I would not bet on a major space launch, a breakthrough AI announcement, or a health emergency. Confidence: low-moderate on specific beats; high that the theme produces at least one or two headlines.

DIPLOMACY will be a background theme and I am less confident about specific developments. South Korea-China relations, ASEAN South China Sea talks (which could not finish this year), India-China border tensions, and Japan's Takaichi attending APEC are all active tracks. I expect a headline or two from each, but none will dominate. The ASEAN talks impasse is a small negative that will be noted. The India-China border flare is a reminder that the thaw is fragile. I would not bet on a breakthrough in any of these tracks during the summit week. Confidence: low-moderate on specific developments; high that the theme is present but secondary.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES THE MOTION MAKES MORE PROBABLE: (1) A new US legislative proposal or executive order on chip controls, riding the political momentum of the Nvidia story. (2) China announcing a new self-sufficiency fund or chip-industry initiative in response. (3) Russia using the summit to announce or hint at a new energy deal with China. (4) A new anti-corruption case involving a senior official, timed to the summit week to show the party is in control. (5) A Chinese military exercise or statement that ripples in the Taiwan or South China Sea context. (6) A significant development in the Nvidia shareholder lawsuit (a ruling, a settlement, or a new claim). (7) A new Chinese export control on a strategic commodity (rare earths, gallium, or a new mineral) as leverage.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full trade war restart, a major military confrontation in the Taiwan Strait, a yuan crisis, a Shenzhou-24 launch, a major leadership structure change (Politburo reshuffle), a formal nuclear arms reduction agreement at the summit, a major epidemic or natural disaster, a sudden large fiscal stimulus package, the trilateral summit being cancelled or postponed, or a second high-profile resignation in the Nvidia story.
crystal.headline: Trump, Xi, Putin Meet as Nvidia Spy Fallout Rattles Markets
emoji_reasons: The first-ever trilateral summit between Trump, Xi, and Putin on November 19 is the single anchor event of the week and will compress the entire Chinese news cycle around it.
The Nvidia spy scandal, from Jensen Huang's resignation to the FBI investigation and Congressional summons, remains the dominant narrative and will drive policy, markets, and diplomacy all week.

China's record $1 trillion trade surplus, the first-ever US-China Board of Trade meeting, and the PBoC's policy support measures keep the trade-and-economy theme steady and prominent beneath the bigger stories.
crystal.tldr: The week will be defined by the first-ever Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit in China on November 19, which will dominate headlines and compress the news cycle. The Nvidia spy scandal will remain the second-biggest story, shifting from revelation to institutional reckoning with Congressional testimony, new chip-control proposals, and Beijing's self-sufficiency response. Trade, Taiwan, and domestic politics will continue as steady secondary themes, with the $1 trillion surplus and Xi's reunification rhetoric providing the backdrop.
crystal.eli5:
Next week, three of the world's biggest leaders — the US president, China's leader, and Russia's leader — are all going to sit down together in China for the first time ever. It's supposed to be about nuclear weapons, but everyone knows it's really about who's in charge and who's going to be friends with whom in the next few years. China is hosting, so they get to pick the rules, the seating, and the photo. Everyone will be watching to see if they shake hands and smile or if someone looks annoyed.

At the same time, there's this huge mess going on with Nvidia, the company that makes the chips that power AI. It turns out the boss of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who might have been a spy for China. He quit. Now the US is investigating, and Congress wants to question him, and Chinese companies are panicking because they might lose access to the chips they need. It's like finding out the person who runs the biggest toy store in town was secretly working for the rival store across the street, and now everyone's trying to figure out who else was in on it.

On top of all that, China's trade numbers are really big — they sold more stuff to the world than they bought, by over a trillion dollars. That's a lot. But at home, people aren't spending as much as they used to, and the government is trying to nudge the economy in the right direction. And then there's Taiwan, which is always on the radar, with China doing military drills and saying they want the island back 'eventually.' None of these things are new, but they all get louder when three world leaders are in the same room.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A correctly identified the Nvidia spy scandal as the dominant story and assigned it 'almost certain' confidence, which was well-calibrated. It predicted Beijing would fire off statements calling the affair a smear and that state media would run editorials, both of which happened. It saw the trade truce compliance process, the APEC summit preparations accelerating toward a confirmed three-way meeting, the PPI spike generating policy discussion, and the Shenzhou-24 buildup including the Pakistani astronaut, all of which materialized. Its 'things not to bet on' list was mostly correct: no full trade war, no major military confrontation, no yuan crisis, no Shenzhou-24 launch, no leadership shakeup. However, A understated the Nvidia story's magnitude, describing it as 'more leaks and speculation' when Jensen Huang actually resigned, was summoned to Congress, and a shareholder lawsuit was filed. It also underemphasized the Taiwan theme, which produced Xi's 'complete reunification' speech and unannounced Pacific military drills described as 'silent intimidation.' The SoftBank-ABB robotics item and the Ma Xingrui-specific angle did not surface as headline stories. A's prediction of a 'verbal exchange with the Philippines or India' in the South China Sea was partially right (India border flaring, ASEAN pact progress) but the more prominent maritime story was the Pacific drills aimed at Taiwan. Overall, A hit the main trends correctly with conservative, well-calibrated confidence levels, but its picture of the week was somewhat flat and missed the color and escalation that actually occurred.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B correctly identified the APEC trilateral summit as the week's gravitational diplomatic center and predicted the logistics friction (the US did balk at China's demand for a tightly scripted format, confirmed by WSJ). It accurately described the Nvidia story's trajectory as 'transitioning from breaking-news mode to investigation-and-consequences mode,' which is precisely what happened: Huang was summoned to testify before Congress, the FBI opened an investigation, the DOJ clarified it had not formally concluded Alice Huang was a spy, and a shareholder lawsuit was filed. B's domestic economy section was notably precise: the PPI complicating policy, the National Team maintaining ETF buying, the IPO halt staying in place, credit growth disappointing, and the car-export data all matched the reporting. It correctly predicted the trade truce holding with the US pressing on compliance and no new restrictions, which aligned with the first-ever Board of Trade meeting and Bessent's calls for balanced trade. B also picked up Moonshot AI, SMIC's profit doubling, and the 'reduce China exposure' theme affecting data-center planning. However, B listed a long tail of specific items that did not materialize as headline stories: Apple's Intelligence AI service, the SoftBank-ABB robotics carve-out, the Macau national-security trial, the Beijing underground church pastor, Papua New Guinea, the China-North Korea meeting, China-Gabon mining, Italy prosecutors, the marriage-rate data, the Taiyuan building fire, the Astellas employee, and the Uyghur men in Thailand. B also underemphasized the Taiwan theme, assigning it 'low-moderate confidence of a major incident' and saying it would 'not bet on a Taiwan Strait exercise,' when the unannounced Pacific drills and Xi's reunification speech made Taiwan a prominent story. The resignation of Huang was a bigger step than B's predicted 'briefing' and 'at least one update,' though B's general arc was correct. Overall, B provided a more structured and useful picture of the week's shape, with better trajectory calls on the dominant stories, but its long list of specific 'possible' items that did not appear slightly diluted its precision.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts correctly identified the week's four dominant themes: the Nvidia spy scandal, the trilateral summit confirmation, the trade truce holding, and active domestic economic management. Both got the 'things not to bet on' list largely right. Both underemphasized the Taiwan theme, which produced Xi's reunification speech and unannounced Pacific drills. Both understated the magnitude of the Nvidia story (resignation was bigger than 'more leaks' or 'a briefing'). The key differentiator is in the trajectory and precision of the core predictions. Forecast B's description of the Nvidia story transitioning from breaking news to investigation-and-consequences mode was more accurate and useful than A's 'more leaks and speculation.' B's domestic economy section, with its specific mechanisms (National Team ETF buying, IPO halt, targeted forex operations, credit growth disappointment), matched the reporting more closely than A's broader 'probable' framing. B also correctly anticipated the Moonshot AI restructuring, SMIC's AI-driven profit, and the broader tech-sector fallout, whereas A's tech section was thinner. On the other hand, A was more conservative and made fewer specific predictions that could be wrong, which is a virtue in forecasting. A's Shenzhou-24/Pakistani astronaut call was clean and correct, while B buried it in a long 'society and misc' list. A's 'almost certain' confidence on Nvidia was well-calibrated, while B's 'high confidence' was also appropriate. B's long list of specific items that did not materialize (Apple, SoftBank-ABB, Macau, Papua New Guinea, China-North Korea, China-Gabon, Italy, marriage rate, Taiyuan fire, Astellas, Uyghur men) is a point in A's favor under the criterion that extra detail only counts if it came true. But B's extra detail that DID come true (Nvidia trajectory, domestic economy mechanisms, Moonshot AI, SMIC, SigmaStar, Anthropic IPO rebuff) was more substantial and more central to the week's actual shape. B also better captured the diplomatic nuance of the summit (the US balking at the scripted format, the nuclear non-proliferation framing, the bilateral side-meetings carrying more substance). For a reader trying to understand what the week would look like, B's structured, theme-by-theme picture was more informative and more accurate on the core stories, even if its periphery was noisier. A was safer and more balanced but less useful as a guide to the week's actual shape. The margin is small, but B's superior trajectory calls on the dominant stories give it the edge.
